title: The SEE Examination: Pattern, Grid and Strategy

toc.title: 1.1 Structure and marking scheme of the SEE
1.2 From marks to a letter grade and GPA

html:
The Secondary Education Examination (SEE) is the first national examination a Nepali student sits, and it is built from a public specification.

The number of questions, their size and the share of marks each content area carries are fixed before the paper is written, so only the wording changes from year to year.

A question bank can therefore prepare you for the shape of the paper, not just for its content.

This chapter lays out that shape for the six subjects in this series, explains how marks become a letter grade and a GPA, and gives a time plan you can rehearse.

Five numbers to hold in your head

75 — external (written) marks in each subject of this series. 25 — internal-assessment marks added by your school. 35% — the minimum on the external paper (26.25 out of 75). 40% — the minimum on the internal marks (10 out of 25).

2.4 — minutes available for every written mark in a three-hour, 75-mark paper. The rest of this chapter follows from these numbers.

1.1 Structure and marking scheme of the SEE

Each subject paper is marked out of 75. Your school separately awards up to 25 internal marks for practical work, project work, class participation and terminal tests. The two parts are graded separately, and both must clear their minimum.

Subject Time External Internal Shape of the external paper
Science and Technology 3 hr 75 25 Group A: 10 MCQ × 1; Group B: 9 very short × 1; Group C: 14 short × 2; Group D: 7 long × 4
Compulsory Mathematics 3 hr 75 25 16 numbered multi-part questions (49 sub-items across Sets, Arithmetic, Mensuration, Algebra, Geometry, Statistics/Probability, Trigonometry)
Compulsory English 3 hr 75 25 Reading 40 marks (2 seen texts 5+10, 2 unseen texts 10+15), Writing 24 marks (5+5+6+8), Grammar 11 × 1
Compulsory Nepali (अनिवार्य नेपाली) 3 hr 75 25 16 numbered questions covering शब्दभण्डार, व्याकरण, पठनबोध, बुँदाटिपोट/सारांश, पाठगत बोध, स्वतन्त्र र व्यावहारिक लेखन
Social Studies 3 hr 75 25 Group A: 11 very short × 1 = 11; Group B: 8 short × 5 = 40; Group C: 3 long × 8 = 24 across 10 units
Optional Mathematics 3 hr 75 25 Group A: 10 × 1 = 10; Group B: 8 × 2 = 16; Group C: 11 × 3 = 33; Group D: 4 × 4 = 16 (33 questions)
Optional Computer Science 2 hr 50 50 Group A: 10 MCQ × 1 = 10; Group B: 10 short × 2 = 20; Group C: 5 long × 4 = 20

Two facts that are easy to miss:

  • Every 75-mark SEE written paper (including Science and Technology) allows three hours; 50-mark elective papers allow two hours.
  • Internal marks are not a safety net you can ignore. A student who scores 40 out of 75 on the external paper but only 8 out of 25 internally does not clear the 40% internal minimum.

1.2 From marks to a letter grade and GPA

Under the Letter Grading Guidelines used for SEE from 2080 onward, external and internal marks are converted to grades separately, using one percentage scale.

Percentage Letter grade Grade point Description
90 and above A+ 4.0 Outstanding
80 to below 90 A 3.6 Excellent
70 to below 80 B+ 3.2 Very good
60 to below 70 B 2.8 Good
50 to below 60 C+ 2.4 Satisfactory
40 to below 50 C 2.0 Acceptable
35 to below 40 D 1.6 Basic
below 35 NG — Not graded

1.2.1 Minimums and NG

A subject is graded only when the external paper reaches 35% (26.25 of 75) and the internal marks reach 40% (10 of 25). Missing either gives NG (not graded) in that subject.

As announced for SEE 2080, a student with NG in at most two subjects may sit a grade-improvement examination; NG in more than two subjects means sitting the examination again in the following year.

Treat this as the rule as published, and check the current notice.

1.2.2 Marks needed for each grade

Because the scale is a percentage, the external paper alone decides the grade you can reach on that component.

External grade wanted Percentage Marks needed out of 75
A+ 90% 67.5
A 80% 60
B+ 70% 52.5
B 60% 45
C+ 50% 37.5
C 40% 30
D 35% 26.25

For internal marks out of 25 the same percentages mean 22.5 for A+, 20 for A, 17.5 for B+, 15 for B, 12.5 for C+, 10 for C (and 8.75 for D, though 10 is the internal minimum for any grade).

1.2.3 Weighted GPA

The public SEE calculators weight each component by its credit hours: 3.75 external plus 1.25 internal (5 credit hours) for Science, Mathematics, English and Nepali, and 3 plus 1 (4 credit hours) for Social Studies and each optional subject.

With two optionals the total is 4\times5+3\times4=32 credit hours. The overall GPA is

\text{GPA}=\frac{\sum(\text{grade point}\times\text{credit hours})}{\sum\text{credit hours}}

A GPA worked by hand

Problem. A student's marks (external out of 75, internal out of 25) are: Nepali 58, 21; English 62, 22; Mathematics 66, 20; Science 60, 21; Social Studies 52, 19; Optional I 70, 22; Optional II 48, 18. Find the GPA.

Solution. Convert each mark to a percentage and then a grade point.

Subject External % → GP Internal % → GP Credit split
Nepali 77.3 → 3.2 84 → 3.6 3.75 + 1.25
English 82.7 → 3.6 88 → 3.6 3.75 + 1.25
Mathematics 88 → 3.6 80 → 3.6 3.75 + 1.25
Science 80 → 3.6 84 → 3.6 3.75 + 1.25
Social Studies 69.3 → 2.8 76 → 3.2 3 + 1
Optional I 93.3 → 4.0 88 → 3.6 3 + 1
Optional II 64 → 2.8 72 → 3.2 3 + 1

Weighted points: Nepali 3.2(3.75)+3.6(1.25)=16.5; English 3.6\times5=18; Mathematics 18; Science 18; Social Studies 2.8(3)+3.2(1)=11.6; Optional I 4.0(3)+3.6(1)=15.6; Optional II 2.8(3)+3.2(1)=11.6. Sum =16.5+18+18+18+11.6+15.6+11.6=109.3.

\text{GPA}=\frac{109.3}{32}\approx 3.42

The certificate issued by the board is the final word; the calculation shows where marks matter. Science, Mathematics, English and Nepali each carry 5\div32\approx15.6\% of the GPA, while Social Studies and each optional carry 4\div32=12.5\%.

1.3 Science and Technology: the grid

1.3.1 Question types

Group Type Questions Marks each Marks
A Multiple choice 10 1 10
B Very short answer 9 1 9
C Short answer 14 2 28
D Long answer 7 4 28
Total 40 75

The board labels these groups in different ways in different papers; this book calls them A to D in the order above.

The 19 chapters of the textbook cover Biology, Physics, Chemistry, Astronomy and ICT, and a typical paper draws on every area.

The MCQs in the CDC model papers are often short scenarios (a lab observation, a number to substitute) rather than bare definitions, so practise using facts, not only recalling them.

1.3.2 What each type asks of you

Type What earns the mark Typical length
MCQ (1) The one correct option; usually a fact, a unit or a one-step calculation 30–60 seconds
Very short (1) One exact word, definition or value one line
Short (2) Two separate points, or a definition plus an example; a one-step numerical 3–5 lines
Long (4) Four creditable steps: an explanation with a labelled diagram, a comparison of four points, or a numerical with formula, substitution, answer and unit 8–12 lines

1.3.3 A time plan for 180 minutes

Block Marks Minutes
Group A and B 19 30
Group C (14 questions) 28 60
Group D (7 questions) 28 70
Checking — 20
Total 75 180

That gives about 4.3 minutes per 2-mark question and 10 minutes per 4-mark question. If a numerical is not working after five minutes, mark it and move on.

1.4 Compulsory Mathematics: the grid

1.4.1 Marks by content area

The CDC grid for Compulsory Mathematics covers 160 working hours. Each area carries marks roughly in proportion to its hours.

Area Hours Questions Marks
Sets 12 1 6
Arithmetic 28 3 13
Mensuration 28 3 13
Algebra 32 3 15
Geometry 28 3 13
Statistics and Probability 24 2 11
Trigonometry 8 1 4
Total 160 16 75

1.4.2 Marks by thinking level

Each area is also split by the kind of thinking asked. The totals across the paper are:

Level What it tests Marks
Knowledge recall a formula, term or definition 12
Understanding interpret, draw, explain, relate 18
Application solve a standard problem 30
Higher ability multi-step or unfamiliar problem 15
Total 75

Sixty marks (knowledge, understanding, application) come from standard material you can practise, and 15 from higher-ability items.

The grid also says a question may link more than one area: an item can start with a Venn diagram and end with a ratio, for instance, with the parts marked separately.

1.4.3 Time plan

Sixteen questions in 180 minutes is about 11 minutes a question, or 2.4 minutes a mark. A question worth 6 marks (Sets) deserves about 14 minutes; the 4-mark Trigonometry question about 10.

Do the parts worth the first one or two marks of each question first: those are the knowledge and understanding marks, and they are the easiest to bank.

1.5 The other four subjects

Compulsory English. The paper tests reading, literature, writing and grammar in separate questions, so the most reliable gain is practice in the skill, not memorising text. Chapters 8 to 10 follow the question types.

Compulsory Nepali (अनिवार्य नेपाली). The paper is organised by language skill: comprehension, writing, grammar and literature. Chapters 11 to 13 mirror it.

Social Studies. Ten units spread across society and socialisation, development, culture, civic awareness, geography, history, civic life, population, economy, and international relations.

Group A asks 11 very short questions (11\times1=11), Group B asks 8 short questions (8\times5=40), and Group C asks 3 long questions (3\times8=24). Chapters 14 to 16 give unit-wise banks.

Optional Mathematics. The paper has 33 questions across four groups: Group A (10\times1=10), Group B (8\times2=16), Group C (11\times3=33), and Group D (4\times4=16) covering algebra, limits/continuity, matrices, coordinate geometry, trigonometry, vectors, transformation, and statistics. Chapters 17 to 19 follow it.

1.6 Strategy that works across subjects

  1. Read the whole paper for five minutes (or use the first minutes of each group) and mark the questions you can finish fastest.
  2. Bank the one-mark questions first. In Science, 19 of 75 marks are one-mark items; these are secured in 30 minutes.
  3. Write to the marks. Two marks means two points; four marks means four creditable steps. Extra lines earn nothing, and a missing step costs a mark.
  4. Show every numerical step: formula, substitution, answer, unit. A correct final number with no working may earn partial marks only.
  5. Draw diagrams in pencil, labelled, in a ruled box. A labelled diagram is often a full mark by itself.
  6. Never leave a blank. An attempt at a definition or a first step often earns a mark; a blank earns none.
  7. Keep five minutes at the end to check units, signs and that every question number is written.

1.6.1 A revision calendar

Weeks left What to do
8–6 Read the chapter notes; do the objective bank for each chapter
5–3 Do the subjective bank in timed blocks; correct against the model answers
2 Sit one full model set per subject under exam conditions
1 Revisit only your error list and the formula sheets; sleep well

1.7 How to use this book

Chapters Subject Contents
2–4 Science and Technology objective bank, subjective bank, two model sets and ranked practice questions
5–7 Compulsory Mathematics the same three parts
8–10 Compulsory English the same three parts
11–13 Compulsory Nepali (अनिवार्य नेपाली) the same three parts
14–16 Social Studies the same three parts
17–19 Optional Mathematics the same three parts
20–22 Optional Computer Science the same three parts

Every question is marked practice: it is an original item written to the pattern. Each objective question has a key with a one-line reason, and each subjective question has a model answer; numerical answers have been recomputed.

1.8 The Computer Science paper

Optional Computer Science follows the 2081/2082 Python curriculum, and its written paper is two hours and 50 marks; the other 50 marks are internal and practical assessment.

Part Marks Made up of
Written paper (2 hours) 50 Group A: 10 MCQs × 1 = 10; Group B: 10 short questions × 2 = 20; Group C: 5 long questions × 4 = 20
Internal assessment 50 practical and project work 35, participation 5, terminal tests 10

The grid fixes the marks of each unit, so every unit, and every unit's long question, must be prepared.

Unit Marks MCQ Short Long
Computer Network and Communication 11 3 2 1
Database Management System 8 2 1 1
Multimedia 8 2 1 1
Programming in Python 12 2 3 1
AI and Contemporary Technologies 11 1 3 1
Total 50 10 10 5
Pass marks on a 50-mark paper

Applying the standard component minimums as percentages, the written paper requires 35% of 50 = 17.5 marks and the internal assessment requires 40% of 50 = 20 marks.

1.8.1 A time plan for 120 minutes

Two hours for 50 marks is again 2.4 minutes per mark, the same rate as the three-hour papers.

Block Marks Minutes
Group A (10 MCQs) 10 12
Group B (10 short questions) 20 45
Group C (5 long questions) 20 50
Checking — 13
Total 50 120

That is about 70 seconds per MCQ, 4½ minutes per short question and 10 minutes per long question.

1.8.2 Revision advice

  1. Run your code. Python and SQL answers are marked line by line; type every program and query into Python and MySQL at least once, and learn the exact form of its output (a pandas table keeps its index numbers).
  2. Write SQL in full: keywords, commas, quotes around text and dates, and a semicolon at the end; never write UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE.
  3. Indent Python correctly (four spaces) and remember the colon after if, for, while, def, try and except.
  4. Learn the full forms and the one-line facts of Networking and Multimedia — devices, connectors, media, IP addresses, file formats — for the MCQs.
  5. Answer AI and IoT scenarios with points that fit the situation, one mark for each point, rather than with a general essay.
  6. Use chapters 20 to 22 of this book for Computer Science: the objective bank, the subjective bank and two complete model papers with ranked practice priorities.

Chapter summary

  • Compulsory and optional 75-mark subjects are 75 external + 25 internal (3 hours); Optional Computer Science is 50 external + 50 internal (2 hours).
  • A subject is graded only if the external mark is at least 35% (26.25 of 75, or 17.5 of 50) and the internal mark at least 40% (10 of 25, or 20 of 50); otherwise it is NG.
  • Grades: A+ at 90%, A 80%, B+ 70%, B 60%, C+ 50%, C 40%, D 35%, with grade points 4.0, 3.6, 3.2, 2.8, 2.4, 2.0, 1.6.
  • Science: 10\times1+9\times1+14\times2+7\times4=75. Mathematics: 16 questions, 49 items, area marks 6, 13, 13, 15, 13, 11, 4.
  • Time: 2.4 minutes per mark. Bank the one-mark items first, show every step, never leave a blank.

Practice questions

Short answer

  1. A student scores 45 out of 75 externally and 18 out of 25 internally in Science. Find the grade for each part and say whether the subject is graded. [2]
  2. Calculate the total of 10\times1+9\times1+14\times2+7\times4 and name the group each term represents. [2]
  3. A student gets 26 out of 75 in the external paper of English. What happens to the subject, and what is the minimum external mark needed? [2]
  4. How many minutes per mark does a three-hour, 75-mark paper allow? How many minutes does that give for a 4-mark question? [2]
  5. In the Mathematics grid, which two areas together carry 28 marks? [2]
Answers

1. External: 45\div75=60\% → B (2.8). Internal: 18\div25=72\% → B+ (3.2). Both clear their minimums, so the subject is graded.

2. 10+9+28+28=75. Terms: MCQ (Group A), very short (B), short (C), long (D).

3. 26<26.25, which is below 35%, so the subject is NG. The minimum external mark is 26.25 out of 75.

4. 180\div75=2.4 minutes per mark; a 4-mark question gets about 4\times2.4=9.6\approx10 minutes.

5. Algebra (15) and Arithmetic, Mensuration or Geometry (13 each) give 15+13=28, so Algebra with any one of those three.
